article.articleHeadline: Australia First Smallpox Epidemic Linked to Colonization - GlobalPost
article.articleSummary: Two studies using disease modelling, archaeology, genetics and historical records conclude that the 1789 smallpox outbreak around Sydney most likely originated with the First Fleet, whose 11 British ships anchored in Sydney Harbour in January 1788. A companion analysis suggests pre-colonial Australia hosted far more Indigenous people than previously believed, implying the human toll of disease and colonization may have been dramatically underestimated. For decades, historians debated whether smallpox arrived with the British or spread south from Makassan traders from Indonesia; the new work points to a British-origin introduction linked to Sydney. The findings emphasize early colonial disease dynamics and how imported infections can reshape populations, with the First Fleet as the probable source of the outbreak that became a defining disaster in Australia’s history.

article.articleHeadline: 100 years of Newcastle disease: How a deadly poultry threat led to modern vaccine tech
article.articleSummary: Newcastle disease (ND) remains endemic in Indonesia, which first described ND in 1926 and today hosts outbreaks in at least 15 provinces despite a general case decline over the past five years. Risk factors include small-scale farming, weak biosecurity, poverty, and intensive poultry movement, with underreporting complicating timely responses as ND signs can resemble other infections. Indonesia designated ND a notifiable animal disease, enhancing reporting, national coordination, and surveillance through a nationwide laboratory network and a digital animal health information system used as an early warning tool. The country now produces over 1 billion vaccine doses annually, including vaccines from local virus isolates, with increasing exports and regional influence. Internationally, the UK’s Weybridge/Pirbright work helped define ND as a filterable virus in the 1920s, catalyzing vaccines and biosecurity advances; modern tools (real-time PCR, whole-genome sequencing, bioinformatics) enable rapid strain differentiation, informing control, surveillance, and trade decisions.

article.articleHeadline: Jiangxi: By the end of 2025, the schistosomiasis epidemic has fallen to its all-time low.
article.articleSummary: By end-2025, Jiangxi's schistosomiasis epidemic reached a historic low, driven by an integrated control strategy that prioritizes source reduction and Oncomelania snail control, aligned with rural revitalization and ecological civilization. Endemic foci are in the Poyang Lake wetlands, along the Yangtze River, and the hills of northeast Jiangxi, with lake and hill transmission requiring different approaches. In lake areas, 90 key towns on the western shore of Poyang Lake have enclosure-and-grazing bans to ensure 100% ban in snail habitats; in hills, site-specific measures (mulch film, drainage) and cross-border coordination with Zhejiang across four counties. Technology supports surveillance: drone and smart monitoring yield a real-time transmission-risk map; a Poyang Lake infection-source platform; and a snail-distribution model using meteorology, hydrology and vegetation. Talent programs (赣鄱血防之星) have trained 500+ people. Next steps: target 11 remaining counties and prevent rebound with new guidelines; public-health culture bases promote ~90% healthy behaviors.

article.articleHeadline: Gastrointestinal Defense Under High Temperatures: Don't Let Your Dining Table Become a Breeding Ground for Bacteria
article.articleSummary: Taiwan faces a summer surge in food poisoning. In July 2025, a Taichung Fengyuan roast-duck shop, after a change of operator, served 64 diners; 53 fell ill and 48 sought medical care, with 41 diarrheal episodes. Simultaneously, 17 Beitou Junior High School girls’ softball players fell ill after a meal, and 18 members of National Taiwan University’s pop-singing club camp were hospitalized after seaweed rolls. The MOH notes May–October as peak season; April diarrheal ED visits reached 125,205, and 113 diarrheal clusters were reported in four weeks. Pathogens such as Salmonella, Staphylococcus aureus, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus proliferate in the 7–60°C “danger zone,” especially when room temperatures exceed 32°C and cooked foods sit out. Five rules: wash hands; use fresh ingredients; separate raw and cooked; heat to ≥70°C; store at <7°C or >60°C; do not leave foods out >2 hours (or >1 hour if >32°C).

article.articleHeadline: Clinical performance evaluation of the Wantai chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay for Treponema pallidum antibody screening in blood donors
article.articleSummary: In China, evaluation of the Wantai Chemiluminescent Microparticle Immunoassay (CMIA) for Treponema pallidum antibody screening in blood donors shows high performance. Using 5,301 donor samples tested with Wantai CMIA and two ELISAs, discordant results were confirmed by TPPA. A reference serum panel of 611 samples assessed diagnostic performance. Among donor samples, Wantai CMIA achieved 100% sensitivity and 99.96% specificity; both ELISAs showed 100% sensitivity and specificity. In the reference serum set, all reagents demonstrated 100% sensitivity, with specificities of 81.25% for Wantai CMIA and GBI ELISA, and 86.72% for Wantai ELISA. The Wantai CMIA demonstrated superior sensitivity and specificity overall and aligns with current blood center ELISA reagents, supporting its use as a reliable tool for syphilis antibody detection in donor screening.

article.articleHeadline: No cough or fever, but weakness all over; an octogenarian man diagnosed with pneumonia.
article.articleSummary: As of July 29, 2026, an 80-year-old man in Zhejiang Province presented with non-specific symptoms—profound weakness, poor appetite, and lethargy—without cough or fever, later found to have severe bilateral pneumonia on chest CT. At Zhejiang Province Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine Hospital (Hangzhou Red Cross Hospital), he exhibited a high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 180 mg/L and a history of atrial fibrillation with a prostate tumor, marking his second pneumonia hospitalization within six months. The case underscores that elderly pneumonia often presents atypically due to blunted cough reflex and immune senescence, with rapid progression to heart or respiratory failure, sepsis, and electrolyte disturbances. Prevention emphasizes vaccination for those over 60 (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV when indicated) and aspiration-prevention measures: upright meals, small, frequent feeds, high-protein nutrition, and delaying recumbency after eating. Families should seek prompt hospital evaluation for abrupt cognitive or appetite changes.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola in DR Congo: They are chasing the virus faster than ever. Are they fast enough?
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak is unfolding in DR Congo’s Kinshasa-Kongo region, involving the Bundibugyo Ebola virus lineage, for which no licensed vaccines or therapies exist. Within weeks, researchers launched accelerated trials: the PARTNERS study evaluating MBP-134 and Remdesivir, and the EBO-PEP prevention study with Obeldesivir, signaling a faster, more professionalized global outbreak response. However, control lags due to undetected transmission chains, late diagnoses, violence, weak infrastructure, and deep mistrust of authorities and aid workers, making contact tracing laborious. The piece underscores that while high-tech medicine, antibody cocktails, and vaccine candidates offer hope, true containment requires trust, community engagement, and robust public-health operations. article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Hopes for protection against the Bundibugyo strain with the existing vaccines against the virus.
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, caused by the Bundibugyo strain, has sparked multiple outbreaks since 2007, including a current cluster in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. Ebola virus disease is a severe viral hemorrhagic fever with multi‑organ damage, vascular destruction, bleeding, and shock, transmitted by contact with infected animals (fruit bats are natural reservoirs) and by close human-to-human contact, especially healthcare workers. There is no vaccine specifically designed for Bundibugyo. An international team tested whether existing Zaire-strain vaccines could offer cross-protection. Using 179 blood samples from the PREVAC trial in West Africa, they evaluated immune responses after rVSV‑based regimens (single-dose or booster) and Ad26.MVA, at 28 days and 3 months. A Luminex assay showed antibodies recognizing Bundibugyo glycoprotein for both regimens, though weaker than for the target strain; rVSV responses persisted to 3 months, while Ad26.MVA responses were stronger at 3 months than at 1 month. It remains uncertain if binding antibodies confer protection; findings published in NEJM.

article.articleHeadline: CDC Has Told Health Departments Exactly How to Handle Travelers Arriving From the Ebola Outbreak Zone
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo (Ituri Province) with spread to Uganda and South Sudan; as of July 23, 2026, 2,905 confirmed cases and 1,269 deaths, the largest outbreak. Symptoms resemble other travel illnesses: fever, headache, muscle pain, fatigue, sore throat, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain; malaria testing advised. Transmission requires direct contact with blood/body fluids or contaminated objects; not airborne. No vaccines or specific treatments approved; early supportive care improves survival. Notable cases: two U.S. citizens tested positive in DRC and evacuated to Germany; France reported an imported case in June. South Sudan is included due to its border with DRC.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola: Sanwo-Olu, NCDC Rally Doctors On Early Detection
article.articleSummary: Ebola vigilance in Nigeria: At the 2026 Annual General Meeting and Scientific Conference of the Nigerian Medical Association Lagos State Branch, Lagos State First Lady Dr. Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu and NCDC leadership urged frontline doctors to recognise Ebola early to prevent spread, noting Nigeria’s 2014 containment credited to early suspicion and decisive leadership amid renewed risk from the Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreak. Dr. Jide Idris, represented by Dr. Olukitan Jinadu, warned that Nigeria’s best defence is clinicians’ ability to distinguish Ebola from malaria in early febrile illness, reinforcing the need for high suspicion after travel exposure. Since WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, Nigeria activated the National Emergency Operations Centre, strengthened airport and land-border surveillance, designated isolation centres, upgraded laboratories, stockpiled PPE and medicines, and conducted drills. Preventing importation and stopping any imported case from causing sustained transmission requires prompt reporting of every febrile illness and travel history, under the THEMES+ agenda and cross-sector collaboration.

article.articleHeadline: Genomic analysis of Streptococcus pyogenes emm1-type isolates reveals M1UK circulation and a genetically distinct Brazilian sublineage - European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases
article.articleSummary: Genomic analysis of Streptococcus pyogenes emm1-type isolates identifies global M1UK circulation and a genetically distinct Brazilian sublineage. With GAS genomic surveillance limited in Brazil, this study analyzes invasive isolates from severe cases and outbreaks across multiple states from January 2023 to November 2024. LACEN/PR received 498 samples from Paraná and eight other states (Minas Gerais, Santa Catarina, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, Distrito Federal, Bahia, Espírito Santo). Of these, 229 were sequenced for genomic characterization (severe disease/outbreak relevance), using Illumina MiSeq, emm typing (emmtyper), MLST, superantigen screening, and Snippy-based phylogeny with MGAS5005 as reference. Of 120 emm1 isolates, 17 were excluded for depth. Conclusion: M1UK circulates among emm1 globally, with a Brazilian sublineage detected, highlighting the need for expanded genomic surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Brazilian wildcats are exposed to diseases due to habitat fragmentation and contact with domestic animals.
article.articleSummary: Brazilian wildcats such as puma, ocelot, jaguarundi, and jaguar face a critical situation from habitat loss, illegal wildlife trade, and human pressure across Brazil’s biomes. Fragmentation creates isolated habitat 'islands' that increase contact with domestic cats and dogs, elevating disease exposure and threatening genetic health. Brazil hosts 30 million house cats and 10 million strays, fueling wildcat spillover and hybridization risks. The Pampas cat (Leopardus munoai), endemic to the Pampas biome, is imperiled by pet theft, habitat loss, road threats, and disease exposure from domestic animals. A 2024 study identified exposure to FeLV, FPV, Canine Distemper (CDV), and Rabies. Rabies antibodies have been detected in jaguars in Pantanal and Emas National Park. Emerging threats include feline sporotrichosis (Sporothrix brasiliensis) and Bartonella henselae. Prevention requires mass vaccination of dogs and cats, habitat protection, and sustained disease surveillance and education to avert declines of Pampas cat and jaguar.

article.articleHeadline: QDENGA Approval Marks New Phase in India's Dengue Fight
article.articleSummary: India’s CDSCO approved Takeda’s QDENGA on July 20, 2026, the country’s first dengue vaccine marketing clearance. Dengue has four serotypes (DENV-1–DENV-4); infection with one offers limited cross-protection, and a subsequent infection with another can trigger severe disease via antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). Dengvaxia’s 2015 safety issues underscore the need for vigilant post-marketing surveillance. QDENGA, given without pre-vaccination screening, showed protection against symptomatic dengue, hospitalization, and severe dengue in large trials, addressing a long-standing India-specific gap. India still reports tens of thousands of lab-confirmed dengue cases annually, with true incidence higher due to under-reporting; climate change, shifting rainfall, urbanisation, and expanding mosquito habitats lengthen transmission. Policy questions include integrating QDENGA into Mission Indradhanush, prioritising high-incidence urban districts, and selecting target groups by burden and cost-effectiveness. The article notes India’s vaccine ecosystem—ICGEB’s DSV-4, Sun Pharma, Serum Institute, Panacea Biotec, Biological E, Indian Immunologicals—and mentions Brazil’s Butantan Institute in the global dengue landscape. Fogging in Ahmedabad on July 26, 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Specialist from HU-UFSCar advises on toxoplasmosis during pregnancy.
article.articleSummary: Toxoplasmosis during pregnancy is caused by Toxoplasma gondii and can be transmitted to the fetus, risking preterm birth, intracranial calcifications, vision impairment, hearing loss, and developmental delays. Transmission risk increases with gestational age, but severe fetal disease is more likely with earlier maternal infection, while late infections more often transmit but cause milder presentations. In Brazil, prenatal screening includes serology to determine susceptibility or immunity; at HU-UFSCar in São Carlos, tests are repeated every two months to detect acute infection promptly and enable treatment. Amniocentesis may be used to assess amniotic fluid if infection is suspected. Treatment is coordinated by CAIC and HU-UFSCar. Prevention centers on hygiene and food safety: thoroughly cook meat, wash fruits and vegetables, wash hands, use potable water, avoid handling cat litter, and minimize contact with cat feces; pet cats do not pose significant risk if not infected. Early diagnosis and prenatal care are central.

article.articleHeadline: Health Update - Brazilian government provides a new vaccine against the bacterium that causes pneumonia and meningitis.
article.articleSummary: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) infections in Brazil include pneumonia and meningitis; between 2023-2025 about 1,400 meningitis deaths; January–April 2026 pneumonia cases reached 47,285. To bolster protection, the government authorizes Pneumo 20 (PCV20), a 20-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, replacing PCV10 in the public network (SUS). It will be offered to children under five and high-risk groups: Indigenous peoples without prior PCV, adults 60+ who are bedridden or institutionalized, and patients with conditions attended at CRIE; more than 6 million doses expected in 2026; private sector price up to R$600. PCV20 expands coverage from 10 to 20 serotypes, notably 3 and 19A responsible for many hospitalizations, and also covers 8, 10A, 11A, 12F, 15B. The vaccine uses a CRM197-conjugated technology. Vaccination uptake has been recovering since 2022; Anvisa approval remains required.

article.articleHeadline: Brazilian spotted fever cases and deaths in São Paulo State, Brazil
article.articleSummary: In 2026, the São Paulo State Health Secretariat (SES-SP) reports 19 confirmed Brazilian spotted fever cases and 18 deaths, a case-fatality rate of 94.7%. Probable infection sites are in ESG Campinas (5), Piracicaba (3), Sorocaba (3), Santo André (1), and São José dos Campos (1); the infection sites for the remaining cases are under investigation. Brazilian spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by ticks, including Amblyomma cajennense. Key symptoms: sudden fever, headache, myalgias/arthralgia, extreme fatigue, and a rash starting on wrists and ankles between day 3–5 that can spread to the entire body, including palms and soles. Early treatment is essential to avoid severe disease. In 2025, 61 cases with 44 deaths (CFR 72.1%). In São Paulo, this disease remains a major epidemiological concern due to high case numbers and elevated fatality risk without timely treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Snake venom breaks the resistance of the schistosome parasite.
article.articleSummary: Researchers from the University of São Paulo and the Butantan Institute tested venoms from eight Bothrops snakes on Schistosoma mansoni, which causes visceral schistosomiasis in Latin America and Africa, assessing effects on gene expression and reproduction. Some venoms reduced locomotion, attachment, viability, and disrupted egg-laying; moojeni venom was most potent, nearly abolishing egg deposition and markedly impairing movement, while jararacuçu reduced egg laying. After incubation, male and female worms were sequenced separately, revealing a systemic collapse in males with many more genes affected than in females. Affected male genes relate to cell division and nerve signal transmission, whereas female changes pertain more to reproductive processes. The study highlights non-coding RNAs as potential therapeutic targets. Praziquantel remains the only approved drug, raising concerns about resistance. Future work aims to design synthetic molecules to target these RNAs and test them in vivo and in clinical trials, per International Journal of Molecular Sciences.

article.articleHeadline: Mizoram Urges NDMA to Declare African Swine Fever a Disaster for Farmer Relief

article.articleHeadline: Infected Girona: The Cholera Epidemic of 1885.
article.articleSummary: Cholera epidemic of 1885 in the Girona province, caused by Vibrio cholerae, spreads via contaminated water and food; incubation 1–5 days with vomiting, diarrhea and dehydration. Originating in the Ganges region, India, the bacterium reached Europe via steamships and railways, with Egypt as an early epicenter (1883) and Iberian cases detected in April 1884 at Toulon and Marseille. After waning in autumn 1884, it resurged in 1885. Spain appointed Mariano Lucientes Pueyo as public health inspector at Portbou to guard the border; passengers from French trains were fumigated and confined, though controls varied at Jonquera and Puigcerdà. In Girona, the epidemic was officially recorded mid-August 1885; main foci were the military barracks, the diocesan seminary, and the hospice. Measures included boiling clothes, burning infected garments and bedding, and repainting beds. Sheltering asylum residents involved relocating 24 infected, eight deaths at Sant Angels. The outbreak subsided and was deemed over by late September 1885.

article.articleHeadline: What is the sand fly that is turning deadly for children? The doctor explains the symptoms and how it spreads.
article.articleSummary: Published July 28, 2026: In the ongoing monsoon season, sand fly infections are rising in Gujarat, India, with several pediatric cases reported in Gandhinagar, Sabarkantha, Kheda, Aravalli and Panchmahal districts. Sand flies are smaller than mosquitoes and thrive in damp, dirty environments, being most active in evenings and nights. Transmission occurs when a sand fly bites a person or animal carrying the parasite Leishmania, then passes it to another person, causing Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar). Children under 15 appear more affected. Early signs include red skin rashes, itching, and swelling; if untreated, fever, weakness, weight loss, anemia, and enlarged spleen or liver can develop, and some patients may have non-healing skin ulcers. Prevention focuses on cleanliness, eliminating moisture, wearing long sleeves at night, using insecticide-treated nets and repellents. Seek prompt medical evaluation for persistent fever or skin lesions.

article.articleHeadline: Chicken isn’t a street vendor; eight lives have been claimed this year, disease spreading in the state | Chickenpox spreading in Kerala.

Common symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, loss of appetite, and a vesicular rash that starts on the face and chest before spreading to the body; lesions become fluid-filled blisters and crust over, with new crops appearing over days. Transmission occurs via droplets from coughing/sneezing, direct contact with vesicle fluid, or shared clothing, bedding, or towels. High-risk groups include pregnant women, newborns, the elderly, cancer patients, organ transplant recipients, and immunocompromised individuals. Severe complications can include pneumonia (especially in older adults), encephalitis (rare), bacterial skin infections, dehydration, and sepsis.

article.articleHeadline: Foot-and-mouth disease ravages livestock! Learn the symptoms, home remedies and easy ways to prevent it; doctor's advice.
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a highly contagious viral illness affecting hoofed livestock, including cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats, and pigs, reported in Kurukshetra, Haryana, India. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive, including mouth cleaning with potassium permanganate solution and applying a borax-honey paste to oral lesions, plus hoof care and fly control. article.articleHeadline: Can manicure and pedicure lead to hepatitis B and C? Hepatologist Dr Amey Sonavane explains
article.articleSummary: Hepatitis B and C transmit via infected blood or body fluids; hepatitis B is vaccine-preventable, while there is no vaccine for hepatitis C. World Hepatitis Day (July 28) highlights infection-control practices. Dr. Amey Sonavane, Apollo Hospitals, Navi Mumbai, warns manicure/pedicure can transmit hepatitis if tools are contaminated and reused without proper cleaning or sterilisation. Reuse of needles or non-sterilised equipment, or contaminated nail clippers and cuticle tools, poses a real risk. Before any procedure, ask whether needles are single-use and opened in front of you, how reusable instruments are sterilised (autoclave preferred), glove changes between clients, and adherence to hygiene procedures. If exposure occurs, seek medical advice promptly; post-exposure hepatitis B vaccination and, in selected situations, hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) may reduce infection risk. No vaccine for hepatitis C; safe practices and early diagnosis are essential.

article.articleHeadline: Interview: What Lakshadweep can teach the rest of India about eliminating TB
article.articleSummary: TB elimination in Lakshadweep marked the first TB-free status for an Indian union territory, declared March 2021. Lakshadweep, a 36‑island archipelago with 10 inhabited islands, faces lengthy sea travel (Minicoy to Kavaratti about 16 hours). India reported about 2.7 million TB cases in 2025, an incidence near 185 per 100,000. In excerpts from Echoes from the Atoll, Rakesh PS—WHO consultant—shows elimination rested on simple, consistently applied actions: annual rounds screening roughly 75% of Lakshadweep’s ~70,000 people, with unwavering continuity of care. Diagnostics were decentralized to islands; sputum collected locally; molecular tests near patients; local treatment supporters managed treatment and follow-up. The sea and monsoon drive logistics, forcing decentralization and frontline autonomy. The piece cautions against direct copying to forest villages like Latehar, but notes these lessons for remote areas: persist with basic, repetitive public-health tasks.

article.articleHeadline: Saraya Agency: "Brain-eating amoeba" .. a rare infection that increases with rising water temperatures.
article.articleSummary: Naegleria fowleri, the brain-eating amoeba, caused the death of 11-year-old Jordan after a Costa Rica family vacation, where he swam in a natural hot spring and later developed headache and fatigue before rapid neurological decline upon returning to the United States. The infection enters through the nose from warm freshwater and migrates to the brain, causing meningitis and encephalitis with severe brain swelling. Globally, 488 cases were recorded from 1962–2023 with about 97% fatality. A recent India outbreak exceeded 200 cases in a single year, the largest known. Scientists link rising water temperatures from climate change to expanding habitats and potentially more cases, including in closed aquatic venues. Early diagnosis is critical; treatment combines anti-amoebic drugs and brain-swelling management. Prevention emphasizes avoiding nasal water entry, using nose clips, and using treated, distilled, or boiled water for nasal irrigation.

article.articleHeadline: Chickens at Risk in the Monsoon! Be Vigilant, or There Will Be Heavy Losses.
article.articleSummary: As of July 29, 2026, during the monsoon in Bilaspur district, humidity in poultry sheds promotes rapid spread of infections among flocks. Without regular cleaning or with damp litter, bacteria, viruses, and parasites proliferate, enabling quick transmission. The most at-risk diseases are infectious coryza (respiratory bacterial infection), coccidiosis, Newcastle disease (Ranikhet), chronic respiratory disease (CRD), and diarrhea. Early signs include reduced feed and water intake, lethargy, sneezing, nasal discharge, facial swelling, breathing difficulties, and thin or bloody diarrhea, with drooping feathers and reduced egg production indicating illness. Coryza and diarrhea pose the highest risk during rain. Prevention focuses on keeping sheds clean and dry, replacing wet litter, providing clean drinking water, avoiding moldy feed, ensuring ventilation, and separating sick birds. Vaccination, strict biosecurity, and veterinary-guided treatment are key to reducing losses.

article.articleHeadline: Three ways to prevent hepatitis B transmission.
article.articleSummary: Vietnam bears a heavy hepatitis B burden: about 7.6 million people are infected, but only roughly 1.6 million have been diagnosed, placing the country among the top 10 globally for HBV/HCV infections. Each year, hepatitis B–related cirrhosis and liver cancer cause more than 1 million deaths. The disease can progress silently for years; liver Kupffer cells coordinate local immune responses, and overactivation can drive inflammation and fibrosis. Prevention priorities: (1) boost immunity via adequate sleep, regular activity, limited alcohol, non-smoking, and a balanced diet; nutrients such as wasabia and S. marianum may help modulate Kupffer cells and limit liver injury. (2) limit transmission routes: HBV persists in blood and body fluids; risks include sharing razors or tattoo/piercing tools, unsterile procedures, and unsafe sex. (3) vaccination: vaccinate unvaccinated individuals and high‑risk groups (healthcare workers, household contacts of HBV patients); pregnant women should be screened to prevent mother‑to‑child transmission. Also address alcohol, fatty liver, obesity, and certain medications.

article.articleHeadline: Proactive Rabies Prevention
article.articleSummary: By 28 July 2026, Vietnam’s National Institute of Hygiene and Epidemiology reports dozens of rabies deaths nationwide, with peak risk in May–August. Dogs remain the main source (about 96–97% of human deaths; cats 3–4%, mainly feral). Lyssavirus transmits via bites, scratches, or saliva on broken skin, and transmission can occur before clinical signs. In dogs, furious form (75–80%) causes roaming and hydrophobia; paralytic form progresses quietly. Humans: incubation 2 weeks to months; prodrome, hydrophobia/excitement, then paralysis and near-certain death. Prevention hinges on prompt wound care (rinse with running water and soap at least 15 minutes; disinfect; do not squeeze or suture) and seeking care within 24 hours for vaccination and possible immunoglobulin. Vaccinating dogs/cats is fundamental; first vaccination at 3 months with annual boosters, especially before hot season. One Health collaboration with WHO and Vietnam’s MoH. Coverage ~56% (2024–2025); target 80% (2026–2030) to end human deaths by 2030. Vaccine: Rabisin (Boehringer Ingelheim, France), licensed by the Department of Animal Health.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue fever is entering its peak season, threatening the community.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever is entering its peak season across Vietnam, with rising case numbers nationwide and more severe admissions in both children and adults. Warm, rainy weather fosters Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, enabling rapid transmission as even small water collections (buckets, tires, vases) become breeding sites. Early symptoms include sudden high fever, headache, muscle and joint pain, and fatigue; the most dangerous phase typically occurs after fever subsides, when plasma leakage can lead to shock and multi-organ failure if not treated promptly. Five warning signs require hospital care: severe abdominal or liver pain, persistent vomiting, abnormal bleeding, and drowsiness or cold extremities. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive with careful fluid monitoring. Prevention centers on eliminating stagnant water, using bed nets, wearing long sleeves, and community-driven vector control and insecticide spraying in coordination with local health authorities.

A shift in dominant serotype accompanies rising infections: DENV-3 accounted for 59.9% of June cases (versus 19.1% in January), while DENV-2 comprised 67.6% at the start of 2026; four serotypes circulate and cross-immunity is limited. NEA data link serotype switches to spikes in cases, though Singapore’s Project Wolbachia vector-control program has helped reduce transmission and lengthen inter-outbreak intervals. Regional context includes Malaysia’s July 9 update with 42,848 dengue cases and DENV-3 dominance, and Vietnam’s >50,000 cases in Jan–May 2026. article.articleHeadline: Be vigilant for typhoid fever during the flood season.
article.articleSummary: Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella Typhi, poses heightened risk during flood season when water and food are easily contaminated. It typically presents with sudden high fever, headache, fatigue, loss of appetite, slow pulse, and either constipation or diarrhea; in some cases, symptoms are mild or absent. Incubation averages 8–14 days. Primary sources are infectious patients; recovered individuals who shed bacteria for 2–3 weeks after symptoms resolve, and, less clearly, asymptomatic carriers who may shed for 2–3 months. Transmission is via contaminated food or water and through direct contact with patients or carriers (feces, waste, dirty hands, contaminated objects). Prevention focuses on surveillance in high-risk, sanitation-limited areas; prompt reporting; clean water supply, waste management, food safety, and environmental hygiene; and public education on cooking, boiling water, and handwashing. Seek medical care for prolonged fever or digestive symptoms to diagnose and treat promptly and reduce spread; antibiotics are used to eradicate the bacteria and prevent complications and death.

article.articleHeadline: 5 facts about mosquitoes that transmit Japanese encephalitis
article.articleSummary: Japanese encephalitis virus is transmitted by night-flying Culex mosquitoes that can travel up to 3.2 km, biting animals before humans. In Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City, six JEV cases have been admitted at Children's Hospital 2 this year, including two with neurological sequelae requiring tracheostomy and prolonged ventilation; another hospital treated seven cases, many needing endotracheal ventilation. Culex activity peaks at night (18:00–6:00) and incubation is 4–14 days; most infections are asymptomatic or mild, but some progress to high fever, severe headache, stiff neck, seizures, altered consciousness, and coma; case fatality in encephalitis can reach 30%, with survivors facing long-term deficits. Transmission cycles involve birds (waterfowl) as reservoirs and pigs as amplifying hosts. Prevention centers on vaccination: Jevax (Vietnam) with three primary doses and boosters every 3 years; Jeev (India) two doses; Imojev (Thailand) two doses or one depending on age. Measures include reducing standing water, nets, screens, and repellents.

Each vehicle comes with medical personnel, sampling tubes and swabs, test kits, PPE, and essential equipment, ensuring safe and efficient operations. Global new infections are about 1.3 million per year; ending the AIDS epidemic by 2030 would require about $21.9 billion annually, which current funding cannot meet.
